name: Jaw advancement for sleep apnea (MAD devices)

lead: Mandibular advancement devices are mouthpieces worn at night that hold the lower jaw forward to keep the airway open. They are prescribed for snoring and obstructive sleep apnea, often when CPAP is not tolerated.
They are connected to looksmaxxing mainly through interest in jaw position and airway; no study has tested them for changing facial appearance.

paras: Holding the jaw forward tightens upper-airway tissues and reduces collapse and vibration during sleep. The effect lasts only while the device is worn.

Reported effects include dry mouth, tooth and jaw pain, and long-term changes in how the teeth meet. Many users stop because of discomfort. Cheap non-prescription versions are unproven, and some specialists consider them potentially dangerous.

lead: A mandibular advancement device (MAD), also called a mandibular advancement splint or oral appliance, is a mouthpiece worn during sleep that holds the lower jaw slightly forward. It is used to treat snoring and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), a condition of repeated airway collapse during sleep [1][2].

The devices are medical products rather than facial-aesthetics tools. Wikipedia reports that the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the American Academy of Dental Sleep Medicine recommend oral appliances for primary snoring and for people with OSA who cannot tolerate CPAP or prefer another therapy [1]. Randomized trials have compared MADs with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) [3][4][5].

The topic appears in looksmaxxing contexts because the same forward jaw position is associated with jaw and airway discussions, and because some people ask whether such devices can change facial structure. No published trial has tested MADs as an appearance treatment.
infobox: Custom or prefabricated oral appliance worn during sleep
Custom devices are prescribed; non-prescription versions are unproven per Wikipedia [1]

paras: Wikipedia explains that moving the lower jaw forward tightens soft tissue and muscles of the upper airway, which helps prevent collapse during sleep and reduces vibration that causes snoring [1]. A trial has compared different mandibular protrusion positions at a constant vertical dimension [6]. Another study used sleep endoscopy with a simulated bite to predict oral appliance outcomes [7].

A randomized crossover trial compared one month each of CPAP and MAD therapy on cardiovascular and other health outcomes in OSA [3]. Another crossover trial compared 8 weeks of each treatment in 59 patients after polysomnographic titration [4]. A systematic review and meta-analysis compared the effects of CPAP and MADs [8].

Wikipedia summarizes that devices work best for mild to moderate OSA, that CPAP is generally more efficacious at reducing apneas, that self-reported use of MADs exceeded CPAP use in some studies, and that a 2024 meta-analysis found about a 66% reduction in the apnea-hypopnea index in severe OSA [1]. A review in the European Respiratory Journal discusses MAD therapy as a non-CPAP option [5]. A study of 630 patients examined tolerability and predictors of treatment success [9].

Wikipedia lists dry mouth, tooth pain, dental discomfort and jaw pain as common issues, and says long-term use has been associated with permanent changes in how the teeth meet; many users discontinue because of discomfort or lack of efficacy [1].

Randomized trials and meta-analyses have compared MADs with CPAP in obstructive sleep apnea [3][4][8], and a crossover trial compared two types of oral appliance [10]. An early study examined a Herbst-type mandibular advancement device for sleep apnea [11]. Registered trials are examining MADs in heart failure, reflux and treatment-response predictors [12][13][14]. These studies concern sleep apnea outcomes. No studies found on MADs for facial appearance.

Community discussion specific to sleep-apnea devices is limited. Jaw advancement as a goal in looksmaxxing is more often discussed through orthodontic functional appliances and orthognathic surgery. Wikipedia notes that cheaper non-prescription devices are unproven and that some specialists consider them potentially dangerous [1].

timeline.event: A study reports the efficacy of a Herbst mandibular advancement device in obstructive sleep apnea [11].
A randomized crossover trial compares two oral appliances for sleep apnea [10].
A randomized crossover trial compares CPAP and MAD health outcomes [3].
A systematic review and meta-analysis compares CPAP and MAD treatment [8].
